steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Latin prose style analyses HOW an author writes, not just WHAT they say. Style includes word order, sentence length, rhythm, and rhetorical devices.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Word order in Latin is flexible and significant: placing a word first or last gives it emphasis. The first and last positions in a sentence are the most emphatic.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Hyperbaton is the separation of an adjective from its noun, which draws attention to both words and creates a literary effect (e.g. 'magna cum virtute' rather than 'cum magna virtute').

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Reported speech (oratio obliqua) allows authors to present events through characters' perspectives, creating drama and showing different viewpoints without direct speech.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: When analysing style, always name the device AND explain its effect — don't just identify it. Say 'the anaphora of 'non' creates a sense of mounting despair'. For word order questions, explain what is in the emphatic positions (first and last) and why the author placed it there. Compare different authors' styles: Caesar is clear and simple; Cicero is elaborate and rhetorical; Tacitus is compressed and ironic. Support every stylistic point with a specific Latin quotation from the set text — vague references score no marks.
